signals.label: Community

signals.label: Ethics
signals.prompt: Ask who owns the models and data, who benefits, and who bears the consequences. Connect AI governance to decisions you can actually make.

signals.label: Resilience

signals.label: Education

signals.label: Empowerment

sessions.title: A FanTrust Conversation with Naomi Klein
sessions.publicBlurb:
Join us for an intimate conversation with international bestselling author and climate justice advocate Naomi Klein.

FanTrust President Catherine Warren sits down with Naomi to discuss her worldview and new book, End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra Taylor. Oligarchs, tech bros, and populist politicians may look like strange bedfellows, but they share an AI ethos and a common toolkit. Together, we’ll unbox it. From harrowing to hopeful, hear how Naomi’s work traces systems of power, who profits from them, and where the rest of us can still push back.

speakers.name: Amber Case
speakers.title: Founder
speakers.bio: Amber Case is the founder of the Calm Tech Institute and author of Calm Technology, whose work gives builders and institutions practical language for designing technology that respects attention, agency, and everyday life. She found the idea in 2007, in old Xerox PARC papers, while writing a thesis on the iPhone. Her institute offers the world's first certification for attention-based design, an 81-point review of how a product treats your focus, and it covers AI products too. She has written four books, including A Kids Book About Technology, and her 2010 TED talk, We Are All Cyborgs Now, has more than two million views. She spent two years as a fellow at MIT's Center for Civic Media and Harvard's Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society. Before the institute she was co-founder and CEO of Geoloqi, a location software company acquired by Esri, and National Geographic named her an Emerging Explorer in 2012.

speakers.bio: Ana Serrano is President and Vice-Chancellor of OCAD University, co-founder of DemocracyXChange, and an award-winning leader in digital media and cultural innovation. She backs the next generation of artists and designers as they take on the hardest problems of the day, from reshaping our relationship with technology to preserving democratic practices.

He created the Community Intelligence framework and has led global communities and developed community and influencer programs across major franchises at 2K Games (NBA 2K, WWE 2K, LEGO 2K Drive) and EA SPORTS (FIFA/EA SPORTS FC). His work spans creator networks, Discord communities, player and design councils, and live-service feedback loops that help teams understand and respond to millions of players worldwide. Community Intelligence asks organizations to stop treating people as audiences to manage and start building communities as living infrastructure: connected, participatory, and capable of shaping what comes next.

speakers.name: Brewster Kahle
speakers.title: Founder & Digital Librarian
speakers.bio: Brewster Kahle is the founder and digital librarian of the Internet Archive, the nonprofit library he started in 1996 to offer universal access to all knowledge. Its Wayback Machine passed 1 trillion archived web pages in October 2025. He studied artificial intelligence at MIT, helped found Thinking Machines, and in 1989 created WAIS, an early internet publishing system. In 1992 he wrote an essay on the ethics of digital librarianship, shipped with every copy of WAIS, that reads like a memo to today's AI companies: serve and protect each patron as if she is your only employer. In February 2026 he tried vibe coding with Claude Code and blogged it as a report on his first trip.

speakers.title: Founder
speakers.bio: Jos Duncan-Asé is the founder, executive producer, and publisher of Love Now Media, an empathy-centered media company in Philadelphia that builds its stories with the communities who live them. It runs a digital newsroom, the print Love Now Magazine, podcasts, and live storytelling nights. In 2024 it published 72 stories and ran an essay series with Technical.ly on AI and the digital divide: the gap between the technologists who champion AI and the everyday people expected to use it. Its public AI policy says nothing AI-generated gets published without human writers and editors signing off. Jos holds an MFA from the City College of New York and studied information technology at Temple’s Fox School of Business.

speakers.bio: Sara Blenkhorn is Director of Innovation at the Buckminster Fuller Institute, where she's redesigning how founders and institutions govern, own, and structure themselves for the AI era. She is a C40 Women4Climate award recipient and has shaped climate policy across multiple levels of government, including Vancouver's Zero Waste 2040 strategy, which she led. Her working belief: design the right conditions, and people show up for each other.

speakers.bio: Brett Gaylor is an interactive media producer and researcher. His recent releases are Field Notes From An Apocalypse, a collaboration with SciFi writer Christopher Brown, Necessary Tomorrows, a speculative documentary podcast with Al Jazeera, Welcome To The Metaverse, an AR project for the 2023 International Symposium on Electronic Art in Paris, and Discriminator, which premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival. His 2020 documentary The Internet of Everything broadcast in more than 20 countries. For Do Not Track, OK Google and Rip! A Remix Manifesto, Brett has received the International Documentary Association award, a Peabody Award, the Prix Gémeaux and three Webbys. Brett has received a prestigious Canada Vanier scholarship for BrainRot Revolution, a creative research initiative to build critical data literacy which formed the basis of his 2026 PhD thesis at Simon Fraser University. Brett is the VP Creative at Hololabs, an award-winning immersive media studio in Victoria, BC, where he recently directed the free-roam virtual reality title Abyss Vault.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival featured speaker square for Brett Gaylor beside a cave workshop whose rock arch opens onto a luminous kelp forest, with the BC + AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Brett Gaylor, VP Creative at Hololabs. He’ll bring 20 years of remix culture, surveillance documentaries, and interactive storytelling to the question of who gets to shape the algorithm.
publicProfile.audienceNote: Twenty years of receipts that the documentary still has a job to do about surveillance and synthetic media, and what that job is now.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Twenty Years of Remix, and Who Shapes the Algorithm

work.label: BrainRot Revolution
work.note: A satirical documentary game: players speed up AI model collapse, then rebuild a better internet from the ruins. The heart of his PhD.

work.label: RiP! A Remix Manifesto
work.note: His 2008 feature on remix culture and copyright, with Girl Talk and Lawrence Lessig. Watch it next to today's fights over AI training data.

work.label: Discriminator
work.note: His 2006 honeymoon photo on Flickr ended up training facial recognition systems. The film traces how, with AI, AR and animation.

speakers.name: Sarah Downey
speakers.title: Founder
speakers.bio: Sarah Downey is the founder of Sarah Downey Consulting, a Victoria practice that helps Canadian nonprofit leaders adopt AI to support the people, values, and missions that matter most. She led three charities as executive director over 20 years in the sector, then almost walked away. She came to AI without a technology background, so she built one, starting with an Executive MBA that taught AI policy from day one. Now she does AI policy and governance work for boards and teams, and she helped build BC + AI's Responsible AI Professional certification. Her argument: nonprofits still hold the public trust on AI that governments and tech companies have lost, so they could lead on governance instead of following.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Illustrated Futureproof Festival featured speaker card for Sarah Downey mending a glowing net on a dusk shoreline with salmon, a raven, and aurora.
publicProfile.profileNote: Sarah Downey, founder of Sarah Downey Consulting, works on AI strategy, policy, and readiness for nonprofits that can’t afford to lose their values in the rush to adopt.
publicProfile.programNote: Sarah teaches the separate Responsible AI Professional course on October 27–28. She has no talk in the festival’s main program.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A way for your nonprofit to take on AI without quietly trading away the values it runs on. Governance for real people, not a binder.

work.label: Nonprofits Could Lead on AI Governance. Here's Why They Should.
work.note: Her op-ed on SFU's survey of BC residents: people don't trust government or tech to govern AI. Nonprofits still hold that trust.

work.label: Intro to AI for Nonprofits
work.note: Her plain intro to AI for nonprofit leaders, the talk her homepage sends you to first. Start here if AI still smells like hype.

work.label: When Builders Show Up for Nonprofits
work.note: She judged five days of builders taking on Victoria's social services problems. One team cut 52 minutes of calls and emails to three.

speakers.name: Philippe Pasquier
speakers.title: Professor & Director
speakers.bio: Philippe Pasquier is a French-Canadian artist, researcher, and professor at Simon Fraser University, where he directs the Metacreation Lab for Creative AI. His work brings together artificial intelligence, computational creativity, and the arts, with a particular focus on human-AI co-creation. For more than two decades, he has developed creative AI systems for music, visual arts, and interactive media, and performed and exhibited that work at Ars Electronica, the Centre Pompidou, ZKM, and MUTEK. His lab also releases tools for artists, like Autolume, an open-source, no-code visual synthesizer you train on a small set of your own images. He directed the Vancouver edition of the International Symposium on Electronic Arts in 2015, and he makes music as Monobor. His research combines artistic practice with critical inquiry, investigating how AI can augment (not replace) human creativity while fostering new forms of cultural expression.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Illustrated Futureproof Festival featured speaker card for Philippe Pasquier in a hat and round sunglasses, beside a cello scroll and a river of musical notation under a night forest.
publicProfile.profileNote: Philippe Pasquier, professor and director of the Metacreation Lab at SFU. He’ll talk about making art with AI without handing it authorship, and what new forms of expression show up when artists stay in the loop.
publicProfile.audienceNote: What it sounds like when an artist keeps authorship and uses AI as the instrument, and a few forms of expression you haven't heard yet.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Making Art With AI Without Handing It Authorship

work.label: Autolume
work.note: His lab's open-source, no-code visual synthesizer. Train it on a small set of your own images, then play it live. Now on Mac too.

work.label: Generative Art and Computational Creativity
work.note: His online course on how machines make art, from chance operations to machine learning, and the arguments that come with it.

work.label: Monobor
work.note: His music as Monobor, back to the early 2000s, with Robonom and Samiland along the way. The artist half of artist-researcher.

speakers.name: Simon Haworth
speakers.title: CEO
speakers.bio: Simon Haworth is CEO of Intellomx, a UK drug discovery company that uses its own neural network models to find the drivers of disease in raw gene and protein data. The company starts from what the biology measures and says flatly that it is not an LLM literature-mining engine. It has run target discovery collaborations with Janssen on blood cancers and, in 2025, with Johnson & Johnson on lung cancer. A British entrepreneur now based in Vancouver, Simon has founded or co-founded 19 companies, including the listed investment company IPSO Ventures, and started the BC + AI Life Sciences group. His case for AI in medicine is augmentation: tools that help people do what they could never do before.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival speaker artwork showing Simon Haworth smiling with a microphone in a checked navy blazer beside a moonlit coastal inlet, under teal and lavender aurora, with coral name lettering, the constellation festival wordmark and BC + AI presenter logo.
publicProfile.profileNote: Simon Haworth, CEO of Intellomx. He’ll talk about what AI is actually changing in drug discovery, where the hype runs out, and what builders in BC can do about it.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A straight map of where AI actually changes drug discovery and where the hype runs out, and a real answer to what a builder in BC can do about it.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Where the Hype Runs Out in Drug Discovery

work.label: AI: Vive la Revolution!
work.note: His 2021 OBN cover story making the case for AI that augments people, with a lung cancer target program as the proof.

work.label: Second collaboration with Johnson & Johnson
work.note: Intellomx’s 2025 follow-on deal with J&J to find and test new lung cancer targets.

work.label: Revealing Causal Biology to Transform Drug Discovery
work.note: The company’s 2026 case for starting from causal biology in patient data, with LLMs kept as helpers, never as the biology engine.

speakers.name: Loki Jorgenson
speakers.title: CTO & Director, Innovation
speakers.bio: Loki Jorgenson is CTO and Director of Innovation at Circle Innovation, where he runs funded programs that help small companies get past their barriers to innovation. Before that came about nine companies over 22 years in Vancouver and the Bay Area, as CTO or chief scientist at firms like LionsGate Technologies and AppNeta, building predictive systems he says we might now call AI. He holds a PhD in computational physics from McGill. He also convenes MAC (Mind, AI & Consciousness), the BC + AI reading group that has held thirteen deep dives on what AI can teach us about consciousness. He has built these systems and still treats what happens inside them as an open question.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival featured speaker square for Loki Jorgenson beside a cedar switchback stair climbing to a roofless observatory under aurora and dawn, with the BC + AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Loki Jorgenson, CTO and director of innovation at Circle Innovation. He’ll get into consciousness, agency, and what it means to build powerful systems when nobody has clean answers.
publicProfile.audienceNote: Sharper questions about what might actually be going on inside these things, and less embarrassment about admitting nobody has clean answers.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Consciousness, Agency, and Building It Anyway

work.label: What Is Consciousness When AI Is Everywhere?
work.note: His talk from February 2026, the night MAC took over the Vancouver AI meetup. A physicist's run at the hardest question going.

work.label: A Conversation on Dual-use and Defence Innovation
work.note: A September 2026 interview on the regulatory bottleneck waiting for Canadian small companies that pivot toward defence work.

speakers.name: Alexandra Samuel
speakers.title: Technology Journalist & Author
speakers.bio: Alexandra Samuel is a journalist and technologist whose AI stories appear frequently in The Wall Street Journal and Harvard Business Review. Her forthcoming book, Working Neurosmart (Simon Acumen, April 2027), shows how to conquer overload by using AI to work the way you're wired, drawing on decades of research on neurodiversity. She built a custom AI coach named Viv and made a TVO podcast about their relationship, Me + Viv, songs about AI ethics included. In 2005 she and her partner launched Social Signal, one of the first social media agencies. She works from Vancouver, wishes she had worried more about social media back then, and writes about how to use AI as an agent rather than a subject.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Illustrated Futureproof Festival featured speaker card for Alexandra Samuel beside a moonlit waterfront writing desk, with the official Futureproof Festival and BC + AI ecosystem marks.
publicProfile.profileNote: Alexandra Samuel, independent technology journalist and author. She’ll get practical about working with AI without handing it your agency, judgment or humanity.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A daily practice for working with AI that keeps your judgment where it belongs, which is with you.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Working With AI Without Handing Over Your Judgment

work.label: Me + Viv
work.note: Her TVO podcast about building an AI coach named Viv and getting maybe too attached. Karen Hao drops by, and so do the songs.

work.label: We Got Social Media Wrong. Can We Get AI Right?
work.note: She helped build the early social web and wishes she had worried more. Her case for being the agent who uses AI, rather than its subject.

work.label: Working Neurosmart
work.note: Her next book, out April 2027: how to work the way your brain is actually wired, using AI to beat the overload.

speakers.name: Sev Geraskin
speakers.title: Co-Founder & VP of Engineering
speakers.bio: Sev Geraskin is co-founder and VP of Engineering at PolarGrid, which runs AI inference on GPU nodes at the network edge, close to users, so voice agents answer without the lag of a distant cloud. He has spent more than 25 years building systems; at Mastercard he expanded distributed data services 100x and cut cloud costs by 75%. He is also president of the Economy of Wisdom Foundation, a Vancouver research society. With co-researcher April Ai he interviewed 51 Downtown Eastside residents about what AI should learn from people, and 43% named compassion, care, or kindness. He works on how the machines run and on whose values they carry.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Illustrated Futureproof Festival featured speaker card for Sev Geraskin before an aurora-lit coastal neighbourhood, with the official Futureproof Festival and BC + AI ecosystem marks.
publicProfile.profileNote: Sev Geraskin, founding VP of engineering at PolarGrid and president of the Economy of Wisdom Foundation. He’ll get into distributed AI infrastructure, community intelligence and who gets to shape the systems underneath all this.
publicProfile.audienceNote: An honest bill for running AI at real scale: what survives the trip from demo to production, and what it costs to keep it running.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Who Owns the Infrastructure Underneath All This

work.label: Whose Values Train AI?
work.note: 51 interviews in the Downtown Eastside. 43% said AI should learn compassion, care, or kindness from people.

work.label: Synthetic Voices Erase Human Texture
work.note: He had four language models play those same residents. Real people hesitate and hedge; the models hand back smooth prose.

work.label: Transmutarianism
work.note: His framework for moral accounting: score a system by the hardship it absorbs against the fulfillment it passes on.

speakers.name: Stephanie Dick
speakers.title: Assistant Professor
speakers.affiliation: School of Communication, Simon Fraser University
speakers.bio: Stephanie Dick is a historian of science and technology and an assistant professor in the School of Communication at Simon Fraser University. She traces the history of mathematics, computing, AI, and automation, and how technologies encode ideas about intelligence, expertise, and human value. She treats history as a tool for the present and brings it to unions, policymakers, and professional leaders facing how AI is reshaping work, creativity, and learning. She wrote Making Up Minds: Computing and Proof in the Postwar United States, forthcoming from University of Chicago Press, and co-edited Abstractions and Embodiments: New Histories of Computing and Society. She has spoken from Prada Mode to the CBC, and has written pysanky, Ukrainian wax-resist eggs, since she was eight.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Illustrated Futureproof Festival featured speaker card for Stephanie Dick in a sunlit cedar forest beside a circular research table, with the BC+AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Stephanie Dick, assistant professor in SFU’s School of Communication. She brings the long view on AI: where our ideas about machine intelligence came from, who gets to define knowledge, and what those histories still do to work and public life.
publicProfile.audienceNote: The long history under the word intelligence, and a clearer view of who got to decide what counts as knowledge and what that still does to your work.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Where Our Ideas About Machine Intelligence Came From

work.label: How AI Sets Limits for Human Aspiration
work.note: Written with Wendy Hui Kyong Chun and Matt Canute: the AI progress story hides a shrinking definition of what counts as intelligence.

work.label: Abstractions and Embodiments
work.note: The anthology she co-edited with Janet Abbate on how computing has served liberation and control, often at the same time.

work.label: Recognition
work.note: Her comic in progress with artist Bren Perez: humans long extinct, the machines still running, one man brought back by a misrecognition.

speakers.name: Taleeb Noormohamed
speakers.title: Member of Parliament
speakers.bio: Taleeb Noormohamed is the Member of Parliament for Vancouver Granville and Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation. First elected in 2021, he is a member of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Science and Research. Before Parliament he built and led global technology companies. He was vice-president of strategy and partnerships for the Vancouver 2010 Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games and directed the review of the bombing of Air India Flight 182. He studied at Princeton and Harvard, then went to Oxford as a Commonwealth Scholar. He is the local MP on the federal AI file, which makes him the person to ask where Canada's AI plans land in BC.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Illustrated Futureproof Festival featured speaker card for Taleeb Noormohamed beside a bright forest salmon river, with the BC+AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Taleeb Noormohamed, MP for Vancouver Granville and Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation. He joins the festival from the federal AI policy table, where implementation, innovation, and public accountability are no longer abstract.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A first-hand read on where Canada's AI strategy is actually heading, and a clearer sense of who it's being written for.
publicProfile.talkTitle: AI Policy When It Stops Being Abstract

speakers.name: Michael Running Wolf
speakers.title: Chair, Board of Directors
speakers.bio: Michael Running Wolf is a computer scientist who builds AI for Indigenous language reclamation, and chairs the IndigiGenius board of directors. A citizen of the Northern Cheyenne with Lakota and Blackfeet family ties, he grew up in a prairie village in Montana with intermittent water and electricity, then engineered Amazon's Alexa and taught at Northeastern University. He co-founded First Languages AI Reality (FLAIR), now run with Mila, which is working on speech recognition for endangered languages that needs far less recorded audio and respects data sovereignty. He also co-founded the Lakota AI Code Camp for Native teens and founded Indigenous in AI/ML. Now in Vancouver and working on a McGill PhD, he builds language technology on the community's own terms.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Illustrated Futureproof Festival featured speaker card for Michael Running Wolf holding a microphone beside a lantern-lit cedar path and aurora, with the BC+AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Michael Running Wolf, board chair at IndigiGenius. He builds machine-learning and immersive technology for Indigenous language reclamation and asks who owns the systems, data, and future those tools create.
publicProfile.audienceNote: What language reclamation looks like when the community owns the model, the data and the future it makes.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Language Reclamation and Who Owns the Future

work.label: Why First Languages AI Can Be a Reality
work.note: His TEDxBoston talk laying out the vision behind FLAIR: voice AI for Indigenous languages, on the community's own terms.

work.label: First Languages AI Reality
work.note: Speech recognition for languages with only a few speakers left and barely any recordings, built around data sovereignty.

work.label: Lakota AI Code Camp
work.note: Three weeks of coding and AI for Native high school students, rooted in the Lakota language. IndigiGenius grew out of it.

speakers.name: Shane Gibson
speakers.title: Founder & Keynote Speaker
speakers.bio: Shane Gibson is a Vancouver sales trainer and author who co-founded Professional Sales Academy, a B2B sales training and AI sales enablement company. He first gave his keynote on AI and the future of sales in 2018, when that was still a novel idea, and it is now his most popular talk. He has written four books, including Sociable! and Real Results in a Virtual Economy: How to Future-Proof Your Business. At a Montreal conference he showed the audience an avatar of himself giving his talk in French and Mandarin, and watched them split between fascination and unease. Will AI help salespeople or replace them? His answer is both. Off stage he's usually in the Coast Mountains with his family.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Illustrated Futureproof Festival featured speaker poster for Shane Gibson beside an antique projector casting a botanical gold beam through a dark, hand-inked forest, with the BC+AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Shane Gibson, founder of Professional Sales Academy. He’ll turn the art of asking better questions into a practical human skill for working with each other and with AI.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A sharper question than the one you walked in with, and the habit of asking it of people and machines both.
publicProfile.talkTitle: The Art of Asking Questions: Futureproof Edition

work.label: Full AI Keynote
work.note: The whole AI sales keynote he gave in Montreal, as audio and video, on whether AI will help salespeople or replace them.

work.label: Why Your AI Tool Isn't Broken But Your AI Mindset Might Be
work.note: Opens on a sales leader admitting Microsoft Copilot made them cry, then shows how a team actually learns to work with it.

work.label: Real Results in a Virtual Economy
work.note: His 2021 book with Denis Cauvier, subtitled How to Future-Proof Your Business: leading remote teams and selling digital-first.

speakers.name: Kristen Delphos
speakers.title: Vice President, Communications and Public Affairs
speakers.bio: Kristen Delphos is vice president of communications and public affairs at UL Research Institutes, an independent safety science organization. She builds its relationships with policymakers, regulators, academic partners, and NGOs, and hosts Here's Why, ULRI's podcast on the science behind everyday safety advice. Before that she led global marketing and communications at Dematic and held communications leadership roles at ABB, GE Industrial Solutions, ADT, and UPS. Her working belief is that science needs more storytelling. Her own team of science writers learned to trust AI by building it themselves, which is the question this festival keeps circling: how people who don't trust a tool come to trust it. She has also written a children's book.

publicProfile.profileNote: Kristen Delphos, vice president of communications and public affairs at UL Research Institutes. She’ll show how a team of science writers learned to trust AI by building it, and what happens when the hero’s journey meets the scientific method.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A way to get a room full of skeptics to trust AI by building it themselves, and what happens when the hero's journey meets the scientific method.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Safety Questions. Science Answers.

work.label: Here's Why
work.note: The ULRI podcast she hosts: researchers take you inside the science behind the safety advice on things you use every day.

work.label: Humanizing Science Through Storytelling
work.note: Her dispatch from Kyoto's STS Forum, where one table turned up three children's books. What it taught her: science needs more storytelling.

work.label: Why ChatGPT Will Never Replace Human Creative Writing
work.note: December 2022, days into the panic: she had ChatGPT argue it could never replace human writers. A time capsule worth rereading.

speakers.name: Kerris Hougardy
speakers.title: Senior Vice President, People
speakers.bio: Kerris Hougardy is senior vice president of people at Ting Internet, an HR and people strategy leader who partners with executives to build resilient organizations through change at scale. She has more than 20 years in HR and an MBA from Simon Fraser University. She is especially focused on the future of work: as technology reshapes organizations, she sees HR leaders playing an essential role in working out the relationship between humans and intelligent machines. In BC + AI's Responsible AI Professional certification she built a reskilling tool that scores skills and roles, never people. A self-described “humanist in a technological age,” she brings the view from inside a company rolling AI out to real employees.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival featured speaker square for Kerris Hougardy beside cedar work platforms floating on a sunrise inlet around a turning basin of coral and seafoam currents, with the BC + AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Kerris Hougardy, senior vice president of people at Ting Internet and Tucows. With Raj Parmar, she makes the case for discernment: the one human skill that cannot be automated, and the one that decides whether AI at work helps or quietly erodes critical thinking.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A name for the judgment that makes you good at your job, and a case for discernment as the one skill that can't be automated.
publicProfile.talkTitle: The Skill AI Can't Give You (And Keeps Talking You Out Of)

work.label: AI Skill-Displacement Risk & Reskilling Navigator
work.note: Six minutes on the tool she built: it reads a role, rates each skill's exposure to AI, and plans the reskilling. People never get scored.

speakers.name: Raj Parmar
speakers.title: HR Leader and Business Partner
speakers.bio: Raj Parmar is an HR leader and business partner at Tucows, where she helps people teams support their workforce through the push to adopt AI. She works with leaders and employees to build AI literacy, aimed at disarming resistance and building confidence so people move toward the future instead of fearing it. She sees humans and AI working side by side: a bot will outwork us every day, but it can't out-human us. She helps people build the skills that can't be replaced, betting the future belongs to the humans who know when to say “wait, let’s check that.” In a room deciding how far to trust these tools, she argues for the pause.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival featured speaker square for Raj Parmar beside a rooftop rainwater commons of planted terraces and collection channels above the city, with the BC + AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Raj Parmar, HR leader and business partner at Tucows. She builds AI literacy inside companies and bets on the people who know when to stop and say wait, let’s check that.
publicProfile.audienceNote: Permission to be the person who says wait, let's check that, and a bet that the future belongs to them.

speakers.name: Dean Shev
speakers.title: CTO and co-founder
speakers.bio: Dean Shev is CTO and co-founder of Virtual Healthcare Technologies, a Vancouver company building ethical healthcare AI for patients. At VHT.ai he leads the architecture of ECHNA, an empathetic care and health navigation assistant, along with the platform’s clinical data systems, privacy-first infrastructure, and Digital Twin technology, which pulls scattered personal health records into guidance people can use. ECHNA is designed for preventive support, not diagnosis. VHT.ai is built to operate under US HIPAA and Canadian PHIPA, with a live iOS beta in the field. He also works in business analytics at Fraser Health’s Centre of Advanced Analytics, Data Science and Innovation, and in 2025 he took first place in Vancouver AI’s data storytelling competition.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival featured speaker square for Dean Shev in a charcoal jacket and open-collar white shirt beside a bright turquoise river braiding over mossy rocks through a sunlit forest, with the BC + AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Dean Shev, CTO and co-founder of VHT.ai. He builds ECHNA, a health navigation assistant that has to answer to real patients, HIPAA, and PHIPA at the same time, which is where healthcare AI stops being a demo and starts being somebody’s medical record.
publicProfile.audienceNote: What it takes for health AI to earn a real patient's trust: consent, privacy law, and somebody's actual medical record.

speakers.name: Suzy Easton
speakers.title: Musician and technologist
speakers.bio: Suzy Easton is a born and raised Vancouver musician and technologist. She holds certificates in Digital/Analog Recording Arts from Columbia Academy and Music Technology from Douglas College. After a recording instructor asked her to pick up the bass and join Seafoam, she spent years playing and touring in Vancouver’s indie and punk scenes. With Minto, formerly the Smokes, she recorded the band’s 2009 album Lay It on Me with Steve Albini at Electrical Audio. She later taught herself to solder and began building and modifying guitar pedals, chasing sounds from vintage fuzz to the Super-Fuzz bass on the Beastie Boys’ “Gratitude,” and sometimes putting the circuits inside repurposed bread toasters. Alongside more than a decade in software QA and technical operations, she now experiments with AI as a musical tool for analyzing, generating and reshaping sound.

publicProfile.profileNote: Suzy Easton, Vancouver musician and technologist. She solders her own pedals, hides the circuits inside repurposed appliances, and treats AI as one more instrument to play rather than a thing to prompt.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A musician's case that AI is one more instrument to play, and a reason to stop calling what she does prompting. She solders her own pedals.

work.label: A Little Louder

work.label: What Would Steve Albini Do?

speakers.name: Ashley Smith
speakers.title: AI Visibility Strategist
speakers.bio: Ashley Smith is an AI visibility strategist and founder of Show Your Proof. She helps professionals identify and close their Proof Gap, the disconnect between their real-world expertise and the evidence available online for AI tools to find, understand, and trust. She came to it after 18 years as a Realtor, including a term as the youngest president and board chair in the 100-year history of the Real Estate Board of Greater Vancouver. She tests the idea on herself in public: one episode of her podcast was recorded on her phone's voice memo app in her Dodge Caravan. She also hosts Canada Now, a weekly podcast of conversations with Canadian founders and builders, from her base in Richmond.

work.label: Canada Now

speakers.name: Ben Shneiderman
speakers.title: Emeritus Distinguished University Professor of Computer Science
speakers.bio: Ben Shneiderman is an Emeritus Distinguished University Professor of Computer Science at the University of Maryland, where he founded the Human-Computer Interaction Lab and directed it from 1983 to 2000. His direct manipulation concept led to clickable highlighted web links and touchscreen keyboards. He conceived treemaps to see what was filling a hard drive, and Excel added them in 2015; a full set of his treemap art prints went to the Museum of Modern Art. His latest book, Human-Centered AI, won the Association of American Publishers award for Computer and Information Systems. A member of the National Academy of Engineering and an early TED speaker, he now lives in Vancouver and argues for AI that keeps people in control.

publicProfile.profileNote: Ben Shneiderman, emeritus professor at the University of Maryland and founding director of its Human-Computer Interaction Lab. He wrote the book on human-centered AI, and he lives in Kitsilano now. He’s coming to make the case for AI that keeps people in control.
publicProfile.audienceNote: He wrote the book on human-centered AI. You'll leave with a clear picture of AI that keeps people in charge, and an eye for the designs that do.
publicProfile.talkTitle: There is No "I" in AI

work.label: Human-Centered AI
work.note: His case that AI can be highly automated and still leave people in control. The book, plus free talks and papers.

work.label: Designing the User Interface
work.note: The textbook behind his Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design, still taught in HCI courses. Sixth edition, 2016.

work.label: Treemap Art Project
work.note: He invented treemaps to see what filled a hard drive, then made them into art prints. A full set of 12 went to MoMA.

speakers.name: Lane Becker
speakers.title: President, Wikimedia Enterprise
speakers.bio: Lane Becker is president of Wikimedia LLC, the Wikimedia Foundation's for-profit subsidiary that runs Wikimedia Enterprise, a platform for organizations that reuse Wikimedia content in their own sites and services. He also oversees the Foundation's Commercial Partnerships division. Before that he was a strategist at 18F inside the US government, where he started and ran 10x, a venture-style fund for public-benefit technology, and Head of Product at Code for America. In his Silicon Valley days he co-founded Adaptive Path, the user experience firm Capital One bought; Measure Map, which Google bought and turned into the front end of Google Analytics; and Get Satisfaction. He co-wrote Get Lucky, a New York Times bestseller about planned serendipity. He says he likes taking money from places that can afford to part with it and giving it to people who can put it to better use. With AI companies training on the commons, that is the job.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival featured speaker artwork for Lane Becker of Wikimedia Foundation, smiling in a dark jacket and floral shirt inside a cedar library with warm reading lamps, the drippy festival wordmark and BC+AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Lane Becker leads Wikimedia Enterprise. Wikipedia is free; keeping it available takes people, infrastructure, and money. He brings a view from inside the work of sustaining the knowledge that AI depends on.
publicProfile.audienceNote: What it actually costs to keep Wikipedia free while everything trains on it, and who is currently paying.
publicProfile.talkTitle: Will Wikimedia Survive the Age of AI

work.label: The cost of ‘free’

work.label: Wikimedia Enterprise
work.note: The product he runs. Five years in, commercial reusers pay for Wikipedia data at scale, and it has repaid its initial investment.

work.label: 10x

speakers.name: Andrew Zolli
speakers.title: Chief Impact Officer
speakers.bio: Andrew Zolli is Chief Impact Officer at Planet, which has deployed the largest constellation of Earth-observing satellites in history. Together, these satellites image the entire surface of the Earth, every day, in high resolution. He oversees Planet's sustainable development, humanitarian, ethics and human rights portfolio, where that imagery, analyzed with AI, goes to work on disaster response, food insecurity, conservation, and monitoring peace and conflict. With Ann Marie Healy he wrote Resilience: Why Things Bounce Back, published in more than a dozen countries. For more than a decade he was the curatorial force behind PopTech, a network of artists, scientists, technologists, and unconventional weirdos. He writes the year with five digits, 02026, a nod to the Long Now Foundation.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival featured speaker artwork for Andrew Zolli of Planet, in a navy jacket and open white shirt on a clear night bluff where a small lit observatory with a brass telescope looks out over a starlit river valley, his name in retro festival lettering with a mint-to-coral gradient, the festival wordmark spelled out in constellation stars above, and the BC+AI ecosystem presenter mark.
publicProfile.profileNote: Andrew Zolli, chief impact officer at Planet. He’ll talk about what it means to photograph the entire surface of the Earth every day, and what all that seeing is actually worth when the hard part is getting people to act on what they can already see.
publicProfile.audienceNote: Why seeing the whole planet every day turns out to be the easy part, and what it takes to get people to act on what they can already see.

work.label: Resilience: Why Things Bounce Back
work.note: His book with Ann Marie Healy, from the coral reefs of Palau to the back streets of Palestine, on how systems thrive amid disruption.

work.label: The Verbs of Resilience
work.note: Is resilience more than a buzzword? His working answer: four clusters of verbs, from sensing risk to learning after a shock.

work.label: Using Space to Help Life on Earth: A Progress Report
work.note: His January 2026 rundown of what a year of daily satellite pictures did, from Amazon enforcement to a Texas methane leak fixed.

speakers.name: Charles Bicari
speakers.title: Systems Designer and Integrator, Research and Innovation Lab
speakers.bio: Charles Bicari is a systems designer and integrator at the Research and Innovation Lab of the Société des arts technologiques in Montréal, building the systems that installations and instruments need underneath them to exist. Trained in electroacoustics at Université de Montréal and in computer science and microelectronics at UQAM, Charles works with AI that is local and small: models running on microcontrollers and Raspberry Pis rather than in a data centre. One project runs a neural synthesizer on a Raspberry Pi 5, its sound steered live by hand gestures. Another passes an image around a cluster of Pis whose AI agents decay and regrow it according to their own CPU heat and load.

publicProfile.profileNote: Charles Bicari, systems designer and integrator at the SAT Research and Innovation Lab in Montréal. He works where electroacoustic practice and small, on-device systems meet.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A way of thinking about AI as a small, local instrument rather than a data-centre spectacle.

work.label: Realtime latent-space synthesis
work.note: A neural synthesizer on a Raspberry Pi 5 whose sound follows your hands through a webcam. The neural network runs on the Pi itself.

work.label: Technocompost
work.note: A cluster of Raspberry Pis, each with its own AI agent, rotting and regrowing an image in a loop. The model runs on the local network.

work.label: Computer vision + OSC workshop
work.note: A starter pipeline for artists: move in front of a webcam and steer sound or visuals through machine learning, without writing ML code.

speakers.name: Toshi Anders Hoo
speakers.title: Principal, Possibility Spaces
speakers.affiliation: Former Senior Research Director, Institute for the Future
speakers.bio: Toshi Anders Hoo is a futurist, technologist, researcher, and the founder of Possibility Spaces, a design strategy studio that helps organizations work through transformational change. He spent a decade as Senior Research Director at the Institute for the Future in Palo Alto, where he founded the Emerging Media Lab. He also served as a media technology advisor to Ray Kurzweil, co-producing and directing Kurzweil’s documentary The Singularity Is Near. His work has been featured at the United Nations, TED, SXSW, Intel, Google, and the Dubai Future Forum. At IFTF he led a W.K. Kellogg Foundation study of what community-centered AI needs, down to local AI and computing sovereignty, the same ground BC builders are arguing over now.

publicProfile.artworkAlt: Futureproof Festival artwork for Toshi Anders Hoo, smiling in his supplied grey zip-neck jacket beside a cyan constellation figure on a bright coastal inlet. Large coral lettering reads The Model is the Medium, flowing into painted turquoise tides above the subtitle The Future of Collaborative Intelligence, with his name, festival dates and BC+AI presenter mark below.
publicProfile.profileNote: Toshi Anders Hoo, principal of Possibility Spaces, spent a decade at the Institute for the Future, where he founded the Emerging Media Lab. He’ll talk about the future of collaborative intelligence: people and AI thinking together.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A picture of what collaborative intelligence between people and AI could look like, from someone who spent a decade researching what comes next.
publicProfile.talkTitle: The Model is the Medium: The Future of Collaborative Intelligence

work.label: The Model is the Medium
work.note: His July 2026 talk in Ashland: treat AI as a medium for people modelling the world together, and keep agency in human hands.

work.label: The Singularity Is Near
work.note: The Kurzweil documentary he co-directed, where an AI avatar named Ramona hires Alan Dershowitz to press for her legal rights.

work.label: Three Horizons of AI-Enabled Work and Workers
work.note: An IFTF report he co-wrote with NTT DATA on where AI takes work next, and why human supervision is likely to stick around.

speakers.name: Dr. Angelica Lim
speakers.title: Associate Professor, School of Computing Science
speakers.bio: Angelica Lim is an associate professor of computing science at Simon Fraser University and director of its ROSIE Lab, short for Robots with Social Intelligence and Empathy. A Canada CIFAR AI Chair, she builds AI that reads facial expressions and tone of voice, so robots adapt to how people communicate instead of the other way around. Earlier she led the Emotion and Expressivity teams for SoftBank Robotics' Pepper humanoid robot. She has pictured robots as kind and compassionate since she was little, and she tested that at home: she and her husband lived with one for six months, and she hosted the French documentary about it. Most of us are only now finding out what that is like.

publicProfile.profileNote: Angelica Lim directs the ROSIE Lab at Simon Fraser University, where she builds robots that read faces, gestures and tone of voice. She once lived with a robot at home for six months and filmed what happened. She’ll get into what living alongside these systems is doing to the people who do it.
publicProfile.audienceNote: What it's actually like to live alongside these systems, from a researcher who ran that experiment on herself.

work.note: Trailer for the 84-minute French documentary she hosted about the six months she and her husband lived with a robot at home.

work.label: On Designing User-Friendly Robots
work.note: Her 2012 TEDxKyoto talk: robots have to earn our trust before they move into daily life, and emotional intelligence is one way in.

work.label: Python Practice Lab
work.note: Her book with Victor Cheung teaches beginners to code by building chatbots, using plain words instead of math.

speakers.name: Kat Koppett
speakers.title: Founder & CEO
speakers.bio: Kat Koppett is the founder of Koppett, a consultancy that uses improv and storytelling to help people and teams perform, and the founder of the Human Interaction Initiative. She wrote Training to Imagine, the applied improv handbook in use for almost 25 years, and co-wrote The Facilitation Advantage with Therese Miclot. Her clients include Meta, Apple, Prezi, PwC, NASA, Global Giving, and the UN Development Fund. She co-directs and performs with the Mopco Improv Theatre in Schenectady, New York, and created Spontaneous Broadway, a completely improvised musical format that made her one of TheatreWeek Magazine's Unsung Heroes. Her career is practice in what people still owe each other with machines in the mix: listening hard, and building on what the other person hands you.

publicProfile.profileNote: Kat Koppett founded Koppett and the Human Interaction Initiative. She uses improv and storytelling to keep people sharp with each other, and she wrote the book on it.

publicProfile.audienceNote: A reason to keep exercising the human-interaction muscles now that the machines are at work beside us, from someone who has spent a career teaching people how.

work.label: The Facilitation Advantage
work.note: Written with Therese Miclot in 2024: a how-to for turning not-so-great meetings, in person or on a screen, into productive ones.

work.label: We Don't Have Personalities
work.note: Five minutes at DisruptHR on why you aren't stuck with a fixed personality, and how practice changes what you can do in the moment.

speakers.name: Anthony Joseph
speakers.title: Councillor
speakers.bio: Anthony Joseph is a Councillor of the Squamish Nation. He has grounded the Vancouver AI community meetups at the Space Centre with Indigenous welcomes, opening the July meetup with hand drum and a journey song, and his talk The Empty Seats Are Never Empty is one of the best things to happen on that stage. He opens Futureproof Festival the same way, with a welcome to Squamish territory before anything else is said.

publicProfile.profileNote: Anthony Joseph, Councillor of the Squamish Nation. He has opened our meetups all year, and the festival opens the same way: a welcome to the territory, the first thing said from the stage.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A reminder of whose territory this is before anyone says a word about the future.

speakers.name: Peter-Lucas Jones
speakers.title: CEO
speakers.bio: Peter-Lucas Jones is CEO of Te Hiku Media, an iwi broadcasting organisation and technology hub in Kaitaia, Aotearoa New Zealand. He leads work on te reo Māori speech recognition, speech synthesis and pronunciation tools, connecting language revitalisation with Indigenous data sovereignty. Te Hiku Media's Papa Reo platform powers Kaituhi, an automatic transcription tool, while Rongo helps people practise their pronunciation. Named to TIME's 100 most influential people in AI in 2024, he asks who controls language data, who benefits from it, and how technology can help a language keep living between generations.

publicProfile.profileNote: Peter-Lucas Jones brings Te Hiku Media's work on language technology and community control of data to Futureproof Festival.
publicProfile.audienceNote: A way to think about AI through living languages and the communities responsible for them, from someone building those tools.

speakers.name: Naomi Klein
speakers.title: Author & Journalist
speakers.bio: Naomi Klein is an award-winning journalist, columnist, and the international bestselling author of ten books published in over 35 languages including No Logo, The Shock Doctrine, This Changes Everything, No Is Not Enough, On Fire, and Doppelganger: A Trip into the Mirror World which won the inaugural Women's Prize for Non-Fiction in 2024. A columnist for The Guardian, her writing has appeared in leading publications around the world. She is the honorary professor of Media and Climate at Rutgers University and is Associate Professor in Geography at the University of British Columbia where she is the founding co-director of UBC's Centre for Climate Justice. Her new book, End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra Taylor, was published September 15, 2026.

speakers.name: Catherine Warren
speakers.title: Founder & President
speakers.bio: Catherine Warren is an international media-tech executive and creative economy strategist, with 25 years at the intersection of innovation, culture, and trust. She is the founder and president of FanTrust, a pioneer in fan-building, digital dealmaking, and urban placemaking. A co-creator of Canada’s first ethical AI accelerator fund, Catherine also co-developed a $100M fair-use marketplace for AI training rights, and advises global media companies, governments, and venture partners on AI innovation, monetization, and digital governance. She is the host and producer of a national TV talk show focused on ethical AI and entertainment, launching October 2026 on TELUS OptikTV. As an economic development executive, Catherine has overseen more than $8B in high-impact investment to Canada since 2018 through leadership roles including CEO of the Vancouver Economic Commission, and oversight of the Vancouver Film Commission responsible for a $4B production ecosystem. Earlier in her career, she co-founded a broadcast software company that went public on Nasdaq and grew to a $300M market capitalization.
